description: We are curious people, that search for new ways to expand the knowledge about the world and ways of help it. We believe knowledge is gold in this world, and we're looking for to spread the knowledge and information, to make missions outside and inside of the world, so much easier. Our group is formed by: 3 engineers, 3 computation scientists.
summary:
We developed an interactive web explorer that lets anyone search the infrared sky for objects that move or change brightness, using real data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. The user enters a position in the sky; the tool retrieves two cutouts of the same field from the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive, taken months apart, aligns them on the same sky grid, applies a common contrast, and lets the user switch between the images and compare them. A pre-processed example keeps the site working if the data service is down.

The project addresses the challenge by turning public but hard-to-use data into a simple visual search for hidden or moving objects, the same principle used to find cold brown dwarfs such as WISE 0855 and in the search for the hypothetical Planet X. In a first test with Barnard's Star, one source shifted about 1.5 pixels (roughly 10 arcseconds) over about 12 months, while the reference stars stayed nearly fixed. This validates the method; it is not a discovery.

This matters because it opens SPHEREx data to students, teachers and amateur astronomers, with nothing to install.
details:
WHAT IT IS?

Our project is a public web explorer for SPHEREx, NASA's all-sky near-infrared spectral survey (0.75-5.0 micrometers). The user enters a sky position (right ascension and declination in degrees).

HOW IT WORKS? (BACKEND)

The backend queries the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 collections, through the IVOA SIA2 protocol and the IRSA IBE cutout service). It selects two exposures of the same field taken months apart by the same detector, downloads small FITS cutouts, masks invalid pixels, reprojects both images onto the same sky grid using their WCS, and applies one shared contrast scale.

USER EXPERIENCE (FRONTEND)

The frontend lets the user switch between the epochs to spot sources that moved or changed brightness. It shows the provenance of each frame (collection, observation date, detector and source link). If the data service is unavailable, a pre-processed real example keeps the site working.

BENEFITS

SPHEREx data are public, but using them requires knowledge of FITS files, coordinate systems and archive protocols. Our tool removes that barrier: nothing to install, no coding, and every image is traceable to its source.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want students, teachers and amateur astronomers to explore real infrared survey data and learn how moving objects are found, the same principle used to discover cold brown dwarfs such as WISE 0855 and in searches for the hypothetical Planet X. It can be used in classrooms and outreach.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

  1. Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript.
  2. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn (Render).
  3. Scientific processing: Astropy, NumPy, reproject, Pillow, Requests.
  4. Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3).
  5. Version control and hosting: GitHub, Vercel and Render.
  6. Hardware: no special hardware; development was done on the team's personal computers at local of presential event.

CREATIVE ASPECT

We brought the classical blink-comparison technique to the browser and paired it with a guided experience for non-experts: one input, two real frames, one clear question ("what moved?"). The explicit provenance panel and the offline example make it both educational and trustworthy.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  1. Scientific validity: same detector, epochs separated by months, shared contrast and masks, so apparent changes are comparable.
  2. Honest limits: in a first test on a high-proper-motion star (Barnard's Star), one source shifted about 1.5 pixels (roughly 10 arcseconds) over about 12 months while reference stars stayed nearly fixed. This validates the method; it is not a discovery. We also saw isolated bright pixels appear in only one frame, which are detector artifacts, not motion.
  3. Reliability: the archive returned intermittent errors (HTTP 503) during testing, and our free-tier server can sleep, so the app handles failures and offers a ready example. - Accessibility and cost: works in a browser, runs on free hosting.

CREDITS AND OPENNESS

Data credited to NASA/IPAC IRSA (DOIs 10.26131/IRSA678 and 10.26131/IRSA662). The code is public. AI USE AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) was used to help draft code, documentation and text.

GitHub link to view the repository: https://github.com/inathanms/projeto-nasa-space-apps

SHOWCASE PROJECT

This is a Interactive Orbital Observatory when you can manually adjust the Earth's position and the satellite's inclination to identify the celestial bodies captured.

As previously mentioned, when analyzing a selected celestial object, it is possible to observe the exact moment and position at which SPHEREx captured the image; this integration was made possible through the use of an HTML-native iframe.

Finally, you can also access information/interesting facts about the celestial bodies captured, as well as side-by-side comparisons of images from different time periods.
